passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of caffeine on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. Sixty healthy adults were randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo, 50 mg caffeine, 100 mg caffeine, or 200 mg caffeine. After ingestion, participants completed a computerized simple reaction time task. The mean reaction times (ms) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded. The results suggest a dose–response relationship, with higher caffeine doses associated with faster reaction times. These findings contribute to the understanding of how stimulants influence cognitive performance and have implications for occupational safety and athletic performance.
stem: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time?
explanation: The table shows the mean reaction times for each group. The 200 mg caffeine group had the lowest mean (250 ms), indicating the fastest responses.
trap: Picking the placebo or a middle dose by ignoring that a lower mean RT means faster responding.

stem: Which feature of the design described in the passage best supports attributing differences in reaction time to caffeine dose?

options.A: Random assignment to four groups, including a placebo group
options.B: Use of a computerized reaction time task
options.C: Reporting a standard deviation for each group

explanation: Correct: A) Random assignment makes the groups comparable at the start, and the placebo group provides a baseline, so differences can be attributed to caffeine. Why the others are wrong: B) A computerized task standardizes measurement but does not address confounding. C) Reporting SDs describes spread, not cause. D) The unit of measurement has no bearing on causal inference.
trap: Crediting the measurement details (computerized task, milliseconds, SDs) with causal inference, when it is random assignment with a placebo group that handles confounding.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time from placebo to 100 mg caffeine?
explanation: Percent reduction = (320–260)/320 × 100 % = 60/320 × 100 % ≈ 18.8 %. Option B is correct.
trap: Using the 50 mg group (280 ms) instead of 100 mg gives 12.5%; the 100 mg group is 260 ms, 60 ms below placebo (320 ms).

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?

options.A: Higher caffeine doses are associated with faster reaction times.
options.B: The 200 mg caffeine group had the fastest mean reaction time.
options.C: Standard deviation increases with increasing caffeine dose.
options.D: Placebo participants had the slowest reaction times.

explanation: The standard deviations fall from 15 ms (placebo) to 12, 10, and 9 ms as dose rises, so the statement that SD increases with dose is not supported. The other statements agree with the table.
trap: Assuming that faster mean times must come with larger variability.

stem: Which description of the dose–response pattern is supported by the table?

options.A: Successive dose increases produced progressively smaller decreases in mean reaction time (40, 20, then 10 ms).
options.B: Each dose increase produced the same decrease in mean reaction time.
options.C: The step from 100 mg to 200 mg produced the largest decrease in mean reaction time.
options.D: The 200 mg group was more than 100 ms faster than the placebo group.

explanation: Correct: A) Mean RT fell 40 ms (placebo to 50 mg), 20 ms (50 to 100 mg) and 10 ms (100 to 200 mg). Why the others are wrong: B) The decreases were 40, 20 and 10 ms, not equal. C) The 100 to 200 mg step gave the smallest decrease (10 ms). D) 320 - 250 = 70 ms, not more than 100 ms.
trap: Assuming that doubling the dose keeps producing equal or larger gains; the decreases shrink (40, 20, 10 ms) as the dose rises.
